en: The Sūtra on the Difficulty of Repaying the Kindness of Parents, Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Parents provide great benefit to their children; they nourish them with milk and food, raise them according to the seasons, and thus enable the four great elements to be formed.”

Carrying one's father on the right shoulder and one's mother on the left, and traveling for a thousand years—even if one were to relieve oneself upon their backs—one would still harbor no resentment toward one's parents; yet even such a son would not suffice to repay the kindness of his parents.
If one's parents lack faith, one teaches them to have faith so that they may attain a state of peace and security;
if they lack ethical discipline, one provides them with ethical discipline and instructs them so that they may attain a state of peace and security;
if they have not heard the teachings, one causes them to hear them and instructs them so that they may attain a state of peace and security.
To those who are stingy and greedy, he teaches to be generous in giving; by encouraging them to delight in such instruction, they attain a state of peace and security.
To those lacking wisdom, he teaches to become discerning; by encouraging them to delight in such instruction, they attain a state of peace and security.

In this way, one has faith in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One; and one has faith in the Dharma he teaches, which instructs and leads to the attainment of the state of peace and security.
All phenomena are profoundly deep; attaining the fruit in this very life is a matter of profound significance and flavor.
Thus, the wise person clearly understands and masters this practice, teaching others to place faith in the Noble Assembly.

The noble assembly of the Tathāgata is exceedingly pure; their conduct is straight and not crooked, they are always in harmony, and they have achieved every dharma—achieving morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation.

What is called the Noble Assembly—the four pairs and eight classes—is the Noble Assembly of the Tathāgata; it is most honored and most precious, worthy of veneration and reverence, and is the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
In this way, these sons should teach their parents to practice loving-kindness. Monks!
There are two kinds of sons:
The son one has begotten and the son one has raised.
These, bhikkhus, are called the two kinds of sons.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves to be like those who give birth to sons, whose mouths produce the flavor of the Dharma.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Difficulty of Repaying the Kindness of Parents.
